summary.text: The finitely many cases \(1\le k\le 59\) are established by direct enumeration; for \(k\ge 60\), apply the hypothesis to the odd number \(n=2k+1>120\). A nonzero determinant forces some binary matrix entry to be \(1\), yielding primes \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\), whose sum (since \(i,j<n\)) is \(2n=4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement for A228623:

\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne 0.
\]

We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

For a positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is

\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Here the subtractions may be regarded as natural-number subtractions, as in the definition of the sequence. For indices \(0\le i,j<n\), they are exact: indeed, \(j<n\le n+i\), so \(j\le n+i\), and similarly \(i\le n+j\). Thus the two numbers in the definition are the ordinary nonnegative integer differences. By definition,

\[
a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

We first record the elementary consequence of a nonzero determinant that will be used. If \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne0\), then there are indices \(i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) such that both

\[
p=n+i-j \quad\text{and}\quad q=n+j-i
\]

are prime. To see this, suppose there were no such pair of indices. Then the condition defining an entry equal to \(1\) would fail at every position, so every entry of \(M_n\) would be \(0\). Since \(n>0\), the determinant of this zero matrix is \(0\), contradicting \(a(n)\ne0\). Therefore at least one such pair \((i,j)\) exists.

For any such pair, the two encoded primes have a particularly simple sum. Because the subtractions are exact,

\[
\begin{aligned}
p+q
 &= (n+i-j)+(n+j-i)\\
 &=2n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now fix an integer \(k>0\). We divide the proof into a finite small case and the case in which the nonvanishing hypothesis applies.

First suppose \(1\le k\le59\). The following table gives, in each case, an explicit decomposition of \(4k+2\) into two primes:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&4k+2&&k&4k+2&&k&4k+2\\ \hline
1&6=3+3&&21&86=3+83&&41&166=3+163\\
2&10=3+7&&22&90=7+83&&42&170=3+167\\
3&14=3+11&&23&94=5+89&&43&174=7+167\\
4&18=5+13&&24&98=19+79&&44&178=5+173\\
5&22=3+19&&25&102=5+97&&45&182=3+179\\
6&26=3+23&&26&106=3+103&&46&186=5+181\\
7&30=7+23&&27&110=3+107&&47&190=11+179\\
8&34=3+31&&28&114=5+109&&48&194=3+191\\
9&38=7+31&&29&118=5+113&&49&198=5+193\\
10&42=5+37&&30&122=13+109&&50&202=3+199\\
11&46=3+43&&31&126=13+113&&51&206=7+199\\
12&50=3+47&&32&130=3+127&&52&210=11+199\\
13&54=7+47&&33&134=3+131&&53&214=3+211\\
14&58=5+53&&34&138=7+131&&54&218=7+211\\
15&62=3+59&&35&142=3+139&&55&222=11+211\\
16&66=5+61&&36&146=7+139&&56&226=3+223\\
17&70=3+67&&37&150=11+139&&57&230=3+227\\
18&74=3+71&&38&154=3+151&&58&234=5+229\\
19&78=5+73&&39&158=7+151&&59&238=5+233\\
20&82=3+79&&40&162=5+157&&&
\end{array}
\]

Every summand displayed in the table is prime. This is a direct finite check; for example, primality of each listed number is established by testing divisibility by primes not exceeding its square root. The largest number occurring is \(233\), so it suffices throughout to test the possible prime divisors \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). The displayed equalities themselves directly show that the sum in row \(k\) is \(4k+2\). This proves the claim for all \(1\le k\le59\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set

\[
n=2k+1.
\]

This integer is odd, and since \(k\ge60\),

\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]

The assumed conjecture therefore gives

\[
a(n)\ne0.
\]

Also \(n>0\). By the consequence of nonvanishing proved above, there are indices \(0\le i,j<n\) for which

\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]

are both prime. Their sum is

\[
p+q=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]

Thus \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes in the large case as well.

The cases \(1\le k\le59\) and \(k\ge60\) exhaust all positive integers \(k\). Consequently, under the conjecture that \(a(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
